highlights: Serene parkland high-rise with sweeping wellness, Thai craft and Bangkok skyline calm
description:
Aman Nai Lert Bangkok rises within Nai Lert Park in central Bangkok, a seven-acre green enclave off Wireless Road in Lumphini, Pathum Wan. The setting places the hotel close to Ploenchit, embassies and the city’s luxury retail districts, while preserving a surprising sense of separation behind mature trees and the heritage house associated with Nai Lert, whose estate has shaped this corner of the capital since the early 20th century.

Designed by Jean-Michel Gathy, the 36-storey address contains 52 suites and 39 branded residences, with hotel accommodation beginning at a notably generous 94 square metres. Interiors favour warm timber, clay and cream tones, deep windows and Thai craft references, creating a calmer counterpoint to Bangkok’s speed. The one-of-a-kind Aman Suite occupies the entire 18th floor, while many suites draw the park and skyline into the room through balconies or full-height glazing.

Dining is deliberately destination-led. Arva brings Aman’s Italian concept to Bangkok, Sesui presents an omakase experience, Hiori focuses on interactive teppanyaki, and the Aman Lounge and 1872 add social spaces for afternoon, evening and club-style gatherings. Experiences extend into the surrounding city through heritage-house dining, craft encounters and private explorations of temples and neighbourhoods.

Wellness is central to the address. The 1,500-square-metre Aman Spa & Wellness centre combines Thai healing traditions with medical wellness by Hertitude Clinic, hydro and thermal facilities, fitness and movement programming, and recovery concepts developed with Novak Djokovic. For Bangkok, the hotel’s rare combination of parkland, suite scale and concentrated wellness gives it a distinctly composed urban presence.

highlights: Three-island Maldivian retreat with luminous reefs, castaway beaches and barefoot Six Senses ease
description:
Six Senses Kanuhura is set in the Lhaviyani Atoll, reached by seaplane from Malé or by speedboat from within the atoll, with a rare footprint across three private islands. The main island is known for its long white beaches and clear lagoon, while one neighbouring islet is used for castaway-style lunches and another is left more quietly to nature. House reefs, turtle conservation and marine life give the setting more texture than simple blue-on-blue beauty.

The resort has 85 beachfront and overwater villas, ranging from one to three bedrooms and shaped for couples, families and larger groups. Beach villas sit close to the sand and palms; overwater villas stretch above the lagoon, many with pools. The design keeps to a relaxed island rhythm, using light timber, woven textures and open-air spaces that feel polished without losing the barefoot ease of the Maldives.

Dining moves around the island mood. The Market serves international breakfasts and changing evening menus; Bottega focuses on Italian recipes, sourdough pizza and Mediterranean wines; Drift turns a private-island lunch into a castaway ritual; Sip & Sand shifts from poolside grills to Japanese-influenced evenings; The Point adds Spanish-style nibbles and a wine bar on the northern beach. Scoops, Sunset Point, beach dining and in-villa menus broaden the choice without formal stiffness.

Wellness follows the Six Senses model of spa rituals, fitness, sustainability and marine education. The spa offers eight treatment rooms, heat and water facilities, an Alchemy Bar, Biohacking Recovery Lounge, yoga studio, gym, tennis and squash. Earth Lab hosts sustainability tours around the water bottling plant, organic and orchid gardens, energy initiatives and conservation talks with the on-site marine biologist. Diving, snorkelling, sailing, kayaking and paddleboarding make the lagoon central to the stay.

highlights: Restored Whiteley landmark blending Bayswater heritage, serious spa culture and West London polish
description:
Six Senses London occupies part of The Whiteley, the reimagined Bayswater landmark whose domed façade and shopping-era history anchor the hotel in West London. The address at 1 Redan Place sits close to Queensway and Hyde Park, with Notting Hill’s colour, Portobello Road and the quieter garden-square rhythm of Bayswater within easy reach. It is a notably different London setting from Mayfair or Knightsbridge, shaped by restoration, neighbourhood life and a sense of urban renewal.

Inside, 109 rooms and suites and 14 branded residences bring Six Senses’ softer wellness language to a restored historic building. The design by AvroKO with EPR Architects favours calm tones, natural materials, residential proportions and greenery rather than conventional hotel gloss. The Whiteley setting adds a strong sense of adaptive reuse: a local landmark recast as a hotel, residences, dining rooms and a membership-led wellness world.

Whiteley’s Kitchen, Bar and Café forms the culinary heart of the hotel, drawing on modern British cooking, seasonal produce, fire, fermentation and instinct rather than formality. The bar moves from classic cocktails to more inventive infusions and natural wines, while the café offers bakes and coffee in a relaxed West London setting. Six Senses Place, the brand’s first members’ club concept, adds social, movement and connection-led spaces for hotel guests and members.

The spa is the defining facility, a 2,300-square-metre wellness address inspired by the atmosphere of an old underground station, with reflection pools, an Alchemy Bar and treatment rooms. Cryotherapy and flotation sit alongside hands-on therapies, while the 325-square-metre fitness centre includes a light-filled studio for aerial yoga. For London, it is a quietly radical arrival: heritage architecture, serious wellness and neighbourhood life woven into one address.

highlights: Hilltop Tuscan castello with ancient stonework, estate dining and celestial countryside views
description:
Castello di Casole sits above the countryside near Casole d’Elsa, in the Siena province of Tuscany, with cypress roads, vineyards, olive groves and wooded hills spreading from the estate. The hamlet of Querceto gives the address its rural stillness, while Siena, San Gimignano and Florence’s airport remain reachable for day trips and arrivals. This is Tuscany at its most expansive: stone villages, pale evening light and agricultural rhythms close to the hotel itself.

The restored castle estate combines suites and villas rather than conventional hotel bedrooms, with 41 keys set within the castello and historic estate buildings. Interiors retain original materials found on the property, from stone walls and timber beams to hand-plastered finishes, layered with contemporary fabrics and country-house furniture. The atmosphere is deeply historic without becoming museum-like, helped by estate details such as the ancient amphitheatre, the hilltop chapel, Etruscan references and the Visconti family legacy.

Dining is rooted in the farm-estate setting. Tosca serves Tuscan cooking in the heart of the castello, framed by stone walls and Italian textiles; Castello Grill looks over the valley with charcoal-grilled meats, vegetables, pizza and pasta; Emporio del Castello uses an old 17th-century wood-fired oven for family-style Italian meals. Bar Visconti and the wine cellar extend the rhythm into aperitivi, tastings and private dinners.

Essere Spa occupies the property’s historic fabric with seven treatment rooms, a couple’s suite, steam rooms and a private garden, supported by a TechnoGym-equipped fitness centre. Days can be shaped around guided hikes and cycling through vineyards, tennis with LUX Tennis, truffle hunting with Lagotto Romagnolo dogs, cooking classes, wine tastings and summer stargazing in the amphitheatre.

highlights: Private Mazzarò beach villa with cabanas, Ionian views and glamorous Sicilian dining
description:
Belmond Villa Sant'Andrea rests on the Bay of Mazzarò in Taormina Mare, with the Ionian Sea directly below its terraces and the cable car to Taormina close by. The setting brings together private beach life and eastern Sicily’s most theatrical landmarks: Isola Bella, Cape Taormina, the ancient Greek Theatre and Mount Etna are all part of the natural sightseeing rhythm.

The former private villa, now a 66-room beach resort, keeps a residential intimacy despite its Belmond polish. Rooms and suites frame either sea or subtropical garden views, with balconies and terraces, marble bathrooms, fine fabrics and a soft Mediterranean palette. The mood is less grand hotel than aristocratic seaside house, where days can move from shaded garden paths to blue-and-white cabanas at Lido Villeggiatura.

Dining is anchored by the water. Ristorante Sant’Andrea serves seasonal Sicilian cooking and just-caught seafood with sea views; Brizza is an intimate waterside venue built around seafood tasting menus; Brace at Bar Sant’Andrea adds a more relaxed coastal grill. The beach bar and pool bar support long summer afternoons, while Etna wine experiences and candlelit dinners on the beach deepen the Sicilian sense of place.

Facilities are deliberately coastal. The ocean-facing spa garden offers single and couple treatment rooms, a sea-view gazebo and Làvika rituals developed for the hotel, while the fitness centre uses Technogym equipment and personal trainers on request. The private beach club brings cabanas, paddle surfing, sunrise yoga and boat excursions on an Apreamare Gozzo 35 towards Isola Bella, Acitrezza or Siracusa. A seasonal Smile Club, children’s menus and family activities make the address as easy for families as for couples.
